title: Pediatric Dehydration: Oral Rehydration Before IV When Appropriate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mild to moderate dehydration is often managed with oral rehydration solution given in small frequent amounts when the child is alert and can tolerate enteral intake. Severe dehydration, shock, altered mental status, ileus, or inability to tolerate enteral fluids requires rapid escalation and IV therapy.
recognize: Dry mucosa, reduced tears, decreased urine, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, weight loss, lethargy, and poor intake suggest increasing dehydration.
No urine for many hours, marked lethargy, weak pulses, hypotension, or altered mental status are late/serious signs.
priorities: Estimate severity using the full clinical picture and trend, not one sign.
Use prescribed oral rehydration in small frequent volumes for appropriate mild/moderate cases; escalate severe dehydration or failed oral therapy.
assessMonitor: Track intake/output, weight, mental status, perfusion, HR, mucosa, tears, urine, vomiting/diarrhea losses, and response to rehydration.
interventions: Offer ORS in small frequent amounts and continue age-appropriate feeding as tolerated per plan; use IV fluids when ordered for severe dehydration or enteral failure.
medicationSafety: Antidiarrheals or antiemetics should not replace rehydration and require age/indication review.
teaching: Use true oral rehydration solution rather than soda or juice for significant gastroenteritis-related losses.
delegationScope: Routine intake/output may be delegated; severity recognition and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Starting IV fluids automatically for every child with vomiting and diarrhea despite stable mild/moderate dehydration and ability to drink ORS.
oneLinePearl: If the gut works and the child is stable, use it; if perfusion or consciousness fails, escalate fast.
sourceBasis: AAP Pediatrics in Review 2025 oral rehydration review

title: Pediatric Respiratory Distress: Retractions Are a Warning
bottomLine: Children can compensate until they suddenly tire. Rising work of breathing, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, cyanosis, altered interaction, or declining effort requires prompt escalation even before saturation collapses.
recognize: Fast breathing, ribs pulling in, nasal flaring, grunting, head bobbing, poor feeding, cyanosis, and decreased interaction are concerning.
A quieter child with less effort can be worse if fatigue is replacing compensation.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing effort, color, mental status, and oxygenation together.
Escalate severe retractions, cyanosis, exhaustion, apnea, or altered consciousness immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend RR, work of breathing, SpO2, breath sounds, mental status, hydration, fever, and response to ordered therapy.
interventions: Position for airway comfort, minimize agitation, apply ordered oxygen/support, and mobilize emergency help when deterioration is present.
medicationSafety: Do not delay respiratory support while waiting for nebulizer or medication effect in a failing child.
teaching: Caregivers should seek urgent care for fast/troubled breathing, blue color, severe dehydration, seizure, or poor interaction.
delegationScope: Licensed nurse interprets deterioration; routine observations may be delegated with clear thresholds.
examTrap: Being reassured by a single acceptable oxygen saturation while work of breathing is worsening.
oneLinePearl: A tiring child can look quieter just before failure.
sourceBasis: CDC respiratory illness emergency warning signs for children

title: Febrile Seizure: Protect the Airway, Time the Event
bottomLine: During a febrile seizure, protect from injury, position for airway safety, time the seizure, and avoid putting anything in the mouth. Prolonged, focal, recurrent, or poorly recovering seizures require urgent escalation.
recognize: Febrile seizures most often occur in young children with fever and commonly resolve quickly.
Focal movement, prolonged duration, repeated seizures, respiratory compromise, or failure to return toward baseline is more concerning.
priorities: Maintain safety and airway positioning while timing the event.
Escalate per emergency protocol for prolonged seizure, respiratory compromise, focal features, or abnormal recovery.
assessMonitor: Observe duration, movement pattern, color, breathing, fever, recovery, and prior seizure history.
interventions: Side-position when feasible, loosen restrictive clothing, protect head, and provide ordered oxygen/emergency medication if indicated by protocol.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics may improve comfort but do not guarantee seizure prevention; rescue anticonvulsants require exact individualized instructions.
teaching: Nothing belongs in the child’s mouth during a seizure; seek care based on the child’s action plan and emergency features.
examTrap: Trying to restrain the child or insert an object into the mouth.
oneLinePearl: Protect, position, time, and escalate if the pattern is not simple and self-limited.

title: Fever in a Young Infant: Age Changes the Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A fever in a very young infant is higher risk than the same temperature in an older child. Infants under about 12 weeks with temperature at or above 100.4°F (38°C) require prompt medical evaluation rather than routine home fever management.
recognize: Young infants may show serious infection with subtle feeding, activity, temperature, color, or breathing changes.
priorities: Verify temperature accurately and assess appearance, feeding, breathing, hydration, and responsiveness.
Escalate promptly for young-infant fever or toxic appearance.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, HR, RR, feeding, urine, alertness, perfusion, rash, and respiratory signs.
interventions: Maintain comfort, avoid delaying evaluation with repeated home interventions, and follow sepsis/infection protocols when indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not give age-inappropriate antipyretics or use medication response to rule out serious infection.
teaching: For very young infants, call promptly for fever rather than waiting to see if it rises further.
delegationScope: Age-risk interpretation and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Reassuring a caregiver because the infant looks fairly comfortable after acetaminophen.
oneLinePearl: In young infants, fever is a risk signal—not just a comfort problem.
sourceBasis: CDC pediatric respiratory illness emergency warning signs

title: Croup: Stridor at Rest Means Escalate
bottomLine: Barky cough and inspiratory stridor suggest upper-airway narrowing. Stridor at rest, retractions, cyanosis, fatigue, drooling, or poor air movement requires urgent escalation and minimal agitation.
recognize: Barky cough, hoarse voice, and stridor are typical croup cues.
Drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance, or inability to handle secretions suggests an alternative dangerous upper-airway process.
priorities: Keep the child calm and assess airway/work of breathing.
Escalate stridor at rest, severe retractions, cyanosis, fatigue, or drooling.
assessMonitor: Trend stridor at rest vs agitation, retractions, color, RR, hydration, and response to therapy.
interventions: Minimize agitation, position for comfort, administer ordered corticosteroid/nebulized epinephrine when indicated, and observe for recurrence per plan.
medicationSafety: Improvement after nebulized epinephrine can be temporary; reassessment is essential.
teaching: Seek urgent help if noisy breathing occurs at rest or the child struggles to breathe.
delegationScope: Licensed nurse must evaluate stridor severity and response.
examTrap: Inspecting the throat aggressively in a severely distressed child with drooling and upper-airway obstruction signs.
oneLinePearl: Stridor at rest is not a routine cough—it is an airway warning.

title: Pediatric Airway Foreign Body: Sudden Onset Changes Everything
bottomLine: Sudden coughing, choking, unilateral breath-sound change, stridor, or inability to speak/cry after eating or playing with small objects suggests airway foreign body. Complete obstruction requires age-appropriate emergency maneuvers; blind finger sweeps are unsafe.
recognize: Sudden onset during eating/play is a key clue.
Partial obstruction may allow coughing; complete obstruction causes inability to vocalize effectively, poor air movement, or cyanosis.
priorities: If effective coughing is present, encourage cough and monitor closely.
If severe/complete obstruction develops, activate emergency response and use age-appropriate choking maneuvers.
assessMonitor: Observe ability to cough/cry/speak, air movement, color, consciousness, and breath sounds.
interventions: Follow BLS choking algorithm and prepare for advanced airway/bronchoscopy evaluation.
medicationSafety: No medication dislodges a mechanical airway obstruction.
teaching: Keep high-risk choking objects away from young children and use age-appropriate food preparation.
delegationScope: Emergency response follows BLS competency and facility policy.
examTrap: Performing a blind finger sweep in a conscious child.
oneLinePearl: Sudden + choking + poor air movement = think foreign body first.

title: Pediatric Meningitis Red Flags: Fever Plus Neuro Change
bottomLine: Fever with altered mental status, neck stiffness, petechiae/purpura, severe headache, photophobia, seizure, bulging fontanelle, or toxic appearance requires immediate escalation and appropriate isolation rather than routine fever care.
recognize: Infants may present with poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, abnormal cry, temperature instability, or bulging fontanelle instead of classic neck stiffness.
priorities: Use appropriate transmission precautions when bacterial meningitis is suspected and escalate urgently.
Support ABCs and prepare for timely diagnostics/antimicrobials per team orders.
assessMonitor: Neuro status, seizure activity, perfusion, rash, temperature, respiratory status, and hydration.
interventions: Institute ordered isolation, minimize stimulation if needed, maintain seizure safety, and expedite provider/RN response.
medicationSafety: Do not delay prescribed empiric antimicrobial therapy for nonessential routine tasks.
teaching: Seek urgent care for fever with unusual sleepiness, seizure, purple rash, severe headache, or neck stiffness.
delegationScope: Isolation initiation may follow protocol; neurologic deterioration requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for classic neck stiffness before acting in a sick infant.
oneLinePearl: In children, meningitis may look like sepsis or behavior change before it looks like a stiff neck.

title: Pediatric DKA: Dehydration Plus Deep Breathing Is a Warning
bottomLine: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, dehydration, abdominal pain, vomiting, fruity breath, and deep rapid respirations can signal DKA. Treatment requires protocol-driven fluids, insulin, electrolyte monitoring, and vigilance for cerebral injury.
recognize: Kussmaul-type respirations are compensatory—not primarily a lung problem.
Headache, slowing heart rate, altered consciousness, or neurologic decline during treatment can signal cerebral injury.
priorities: Escalate suspected DKA promptly and obtain ordered glucose/ketone/electrolyte data without delaying stabilization.
Monitor neurologic status carefully during therapy.
assessMonitor: Glucose, ketones, electrolytes, hydration, urine, VS, respirations, and neuro status.
interventions: Follow pediatric DKA protocol for fluids, insulin, potassium, and monitoring; avoid unsupervised rapid correction.
medicationSafety: IV insulin and electrolyte replacement are high-alert therapies requiring protocol and appropriate scope.
teaching: Sick-day plans and ketone checks help catch DKA before severe dehydration develops.
delegationScope: High-alert infusion management varies by state/facility; deterioration requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Treating deep breathing as asthma without considering metabolic acidosis in a dehydrated child with hyperglycemia symptoms.
oneLinePearl: DKA can look respiratory because the lungs are compensating for acid.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Pediatric Sepsis: Behavior and Perfusion Can Change First
bottomLine: Pediatric sepsis may present with altered interaction, poor feeding, abnormal temperature, tachycardia, tachypnea, mottling, delayed capillary refill, decreased urine, or hypotension. Hypotension is late—do not wait for it before escalating suspected shock.
recognize: Children may maintain BP despite worsening perfusion.
Fever is not required; hypothermia can also signal serious infection.
priorities: Escalate suspected sepsis/shock immediately and support ABCs/perfusion.
Prepare for time-sensitive cultures, antibiotics, fluids, and monitoring per pediatric protocol.
assessMonitor: Mental status, capillary refill, pulses, skin, HR, RR, BP, urine, temperature, oxygenation, and response to treatment.
interventions: Follow sepsis pathway and reassess frequently after each intervention.
medicationSafety: Weight-based emergency medications/fluids require current measured kilograms and protocol verification.
teaching: Caregivers should seek urgent care when a child is hard to wake, not interacting, not urinating, or struggling to breathe.
delegationScope: Sepsis recognition and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Waiting for low blood pressure before calling pediatric shock.
oneLinePearl: In children, poor perfusion can be severe before BP falls.

title: Intussusception: Episodic Pain Can Hide a Surgical Abdomen
bottomLine: Intermittent severe abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, lethargy, abdominal mass, or bloody/mucous stool suggests intussusception. A child who looks well between episodes can still have bowel ischemia risk.
recognize: Pain may be episodic with quiet intervals.
Bloody 'currant jelly' stool is a later clue and should not be required before escalating suspicion.
priorities: Keep NPO and escalate promptly for diagnostic/reduction treatment.
Monitor for perforation, shock, or peritonitis.
assessMonitor: Pain pattern, vomiting, stool, abdominal distention/tenderness, hydration, VS, and perfusion.
interventions: Maintain IV/fluids as ordered, prepare for imaging/enema reduction or surgery, and avoid unnecessary oral intake.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not delay diagnostic escalation; avoid laxatives/enemas outside prescribed reduction procedures.
teaching: Recurrent episodic severe pain in a young child warrants prompt assessment even if the child temporarily settles.
delegationScope: Licensed nurse evaluates abdominal deterioration and keeps surgical concerns escalated.
examTrap: Waiting for classic bloody stool before considering intussusception.
oneLinePearl: Pain that comes and goes can still be a bowel emergency.
